screens.title: Hardwired Control Unit Design
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore how a hardwired control unit converts an instruction opcode into the control signals that drive every part of the datapath. You will learn what each common signal does, how to build a truth table that maps instruction types to signals, and how to turn that truth table into Boolean equations implemented with AND, OR and NOT gates. We will also examine the programmable logic array, a compact, regular way to implement many control equations, and contrast the performance and flexibility trade-offs compared with microcoded control. A concrete example will show how ADD, LW, SW and BEQ set RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, ALUSrc, MemtoReg, Branch and ALUOp lines. By the end, you should be able to design a truth table for a small instruction set and select an implementation style — gate logic or PLA — based on speed and ease of change. A common misconception is that faster always means more complex; we will see situations where a small, fixed ISA benefits from very fast hardwired logic, and other cases where microcode is the sensible choice. Think about an instruction your processor uses: what signals must it set? That question guides design.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will design a hardwired control unit and reason about its trade-offs. First, you will learn to create a truth table that maps instruction opcodes to the set of control signals required for execution, which is a concrete skill for translating ISA semantics into hardware. Second, you will derive Boolean equations from that truth table and express each control signal as a logical combination of decoded instruction-type signals; this skill directly supports gate-level implementation. Third, you will implement the control logic in hardware either with AND-OR gate networks or by programming a PLA, gaining practical experience with two common implementation patterns. Fourth, you will analyze speed, flexibility, and complexity trade-offs and decide when hardwired control is appropriate versus when microcode is preferable. Each objective includes a short practice — build a truth table for five instructions, derive equations, implement on a PLA schematic, and estimate propagation delay. These objectives matter because control logic governs instruction latency and hardware verification effort. Ask yourself: which objective will help you most when adding a new instruction to an ISA?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: This page lays out the concrete practice you will use to verify your competency. Start by designing a truth table for five instructions — ADD, SUB, LW, SW and BEQ — and list the control signals active in each instruction. Next, derive Boolean equations from that truth table and test them by checking each instruction row. Then implement the same equations two ways: by wiring AND and OR gates, and by programming a small PLA with AND and OR planes. Finally, analyze delays by assuming a 1-nanosecond delay per gate and summing gate levels along the longest control path. These exercises teach you how to translate ISA semantics into hardware, how to choose an implementation style, and how to estimate performance. For assessment, you will explain why a PLA is a good choice for RISC and why early CISC designs used microcode. Practicing these tasks builds both design intuition and practical verification skills. Which exercise will you tackle first — truth tables, equations, PLA wiring, or delay calculation?

screens.title: What the Control Unit Does
screens.narratorSegment: The control unit orchestrates every step of instruction execution by producing control signals that open and close datapath elements. Concretely, control signals enable register writes, gate ALU inputs, choose memory access, and select the next program counter. For example, when the LW instruction executes, MemRead and MemtoReg must be active so that data memory is read and the loaded word is written back into the register file. When an ADD instruction runs, RegWrite is enabled but MemRead and MemWrite are disabled; ALUSrc selects register operands and the ALU performs addition. A hardwired control unit implements these mappings using purely combinational logic: the opcode is decoded into instruction-type lines and those lines feed combinational expressions that produce each control signal. A common misconception is that the control unit stores behavior like a program — it doesn't. Hardwired control is not sequential microcode; it computes outputs directly from opcode and, for multi-cycle designs, the current state. Understanding this difference is crucial when you interpret why PLAs or gate networks are used for speed and why microcode is used when instructions are complex. Consider: what signals must your processor assert when it executes a load instruction?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: The control unit translates opcode and state into the control signals that steer the datapath and memory.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What the Control Unit Does
Control unit: role and behavior
Generates RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, ALUSrc, MemtoReg, Branch, ALUOp, and PCSrc from opcode and state.
Example: LW
MemRead = 1, MemtoReg = 1, RegWrite = 1, ALUSrc = 1. The ALU computes address, memory is read, result written to register.
Example: ADD
RegWrite = 1, ALUSrc = 0, MemRead/MemWrite = 0. The ALU performs arithmetic and the result is written back.
Common misconception
Hardwired control computes outputs from the opcode and state; it does not fetch microinstructions. This is why it is fast but less flexible.
Concrete signal list
  • RegWrite — enable register file write
  • MemRead / MemWrite — data memory access
  • ALUSrc — select second ALU operand
  • MemtoReg — choose register write source
  • Branch, ALUOp, PCSrc — control flow and ALU selection
Key Takeaway

Control signals encode the precise actions the datapath must take; hardwired logic produces them directly and quickly.

screens.title: Truth Table: Mapping Instructions to Signals
screens.narratorSegment: A truth table is the explicit mapping from each instruction type to the control signals that must be asserted. Building this table forces you to think through the datapath actions for each instruction. For example, using a small instruction set we list rows for ADD, LW, SW and BEQ and mark whether RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, ALUSrc, MemtoReg and Branch are active. This table also includes ALUOp bits that the ALU control uses to select operations. As you construct the table, check the semantics: loads require a memory read and a register write, stores require a memory write and no register write, arithmetic instructions write registers but do not touch memory, and branches assert Branch but not RegWrite. A frequent error is leaving don't-care values undefined; mark them as X only when the datapath truly ignores the signal. Use the truth table to verify your intuition before deriving equations. Below is a compact, code-style representation of the truth table and the standard row-to-equation correspondence you will use when synthesizing logic. Truth Table: Mapping Instructions to Signals means the truth table is the authoritative mapping of instruction types to control outputs and is the source for boolean equations.. In practical terms, build the table that is the foundation of control logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Truth table
keyIdea.text: The truth table is the authoritative mapping of instruction types to control outputs and is the source for Boolean equations.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Truth Table
Truth table (compact)
Rows list instruction and control outputs used to derive equations.
Instruction | RegWrite MemRead MemWrite ALUSrc MemtoReg Branch ALUOp
ADD         | 1       0       0       0      0        0      10
LW          | 1       1       0       1      1        0      00
SW          | 0       0       1       1      X        0      00
BEQ         | 0       0       0       0      X        1      01
How to use the table
  • Verify datapath semantics for each instruction before converting to equations.
  • Mark don't-care values as X only when safe.
  • Use decoded instruction signals (e.g., ADD, LW) as product terms to build outputs.
Concrete example
For LW: RegWrite = 1 because the load writes the register, MemRead = 1 to read data memory, MemtoReg = 1 to route memory data to the register file.
Check your understanding

Why is ALUSrc = 1 for LW and SW but 0 for ADD?

screens.title: Deriving Boolean Equations
screens.narratorSegment: Once the truth table is complete, derive Boolean equations that express each control signal as a logical sum of product terms corresponding to instruction-type signals. The standard process: first decode the opcode into named signals such as ADD, LW, SW, BEQ. Then, for each control output, list the rows where the output is asserted and create product terms that correspond to those instruction signals. For example, RegWrite is asserted for ADD and LW, so RegWrite = ADD OR LW. ALUSrc is asserted for LW and SW, so ALUSrc = LW OR SW. MemtoReg = LW. Branch = BEQ. For ALUOp you can use bit-level outputs: ALUOp1 = ADD; ALUOp0 = BEQ. Implementing these equations directly with AND and OR gates is straightforward: the decoder provides the instruction signals and the OR plane sums them. A common pitfall is failing to factor common terms when scaling to many instructions — factoring reduces gate count and improves delay. Below is a small set of equations you will implement, and then we will show how a PLA realizes the same sums of products in a structured array.

keyIdea.title: Equation method
keyIdea.text: Decode opcodes to instruction signals; express each control output as an OR of instruction product terms that assert it.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Deriving Boolean Equations
Boolean equations (derived)
RegWrite = ADD + LW
MemRead  = LW
MemWrite = SW
ALUSrc   = LW + SW
MemtoReg = LW
Branch   = BEQ
ALUOp1   = ADD
ALUOp0   = BEQ
Plus signs mean logical OR, concatenation or product terms are used when needed. Use the decoder to assert ADD, LW, SW, BEQ signals from the opcode bits.
Implementation notes
  • Decoder converts opcode to instruction signals used as inputs to OR gates.
  • Factor common signals to reduce OR fan-in and gate levels for speed.
  • For multi-cycle control include state bits in product terms to vary outputs by stage.
Misconception
Equations are not code; they represent structural wiring you implement with gates or a PLA.

screens.title: Decoder and Instruction Signals
screens.narratorSegment: A decoder translates opcode bit patterns into distinct instruction-type signals such as ADD, LW, SW and BEQ. These decoded lines become the simplest inputs to the control equations. The decoder may be a small combinational block that compares opcode bits and asserts exactly one instruction line for fixed-length opcodes. Using decoded signals simplifies the control equations by removing opcode bit-level conditions from every expression. For example, instead of writing RegWrite = (opcode == binary for ADD) OR (opcode == binary for LW) you implement a decoder that outputs ADD or LW and then RegWrite = ADD OR LW. This separation also helps verification: you can test the decoder independently and then verify that the OR/AND network uses those signals correctly. In multi-cycle designs the decoder outputs are often ANDed with the state bits from the finite state machine so that control signals are asserted only in the correct pipeline stage. A common error is to forget to mask decoded signals by state when control is stage-dependent — this leads to transient or persistent wrong signals. Think through the decoder output for each opcode you expect to support.

keyIdea.title: Decoder role
keyIdea.text: Decode opcode into orthogonal instruction signals to simplify control equations and verification; combine with state bits for stage-dependent control.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Decoder and Instruction Signals
Decoder: opcode → instruction signals
A small combinational block asserts named instruction lines used by control equations.
Benefits
  • Simpler boolean equations
  • Independent testing of decoder and control logic
  • Easier factoring and optimization
Stage-dependent control
AND decoded instruction signals with state bits to produce outputs only in intended stages, e.g., enable RegWrite in WB stage only.
Concrete example
If the decoder asserts LW and the state equals WB, then RegWrite = LW AND WB. Without the WB mask a load might attempt to write too early or at the wrong time.
Decoder outputs
ADD, SUB, LW, SW, BEQ — each is a decoded line used in equations.
Key Takeaway

Decoding separates opcode decoding from control logic and simplifies design and verification.

screens.title: Implementing Equations with AND-OR Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing control equations with AND and OR gates is the most direct path from Boolean expressions to hardware. Each product term is an AND of decoded signals (or decoded signals combined with state bits), and OR gates sum the needed product terms for each control output. When you wire the network, consider gate fan-in and gate delays: large multi-input ORs increase propagation delay and may need to be balanced by factoring expressions or using tree structures. For example, RegWrite = ADD OR LW is a simple two-input OR. In contrast, a control signal asserted by many instruction types will produce an OR with many inputs; factor or group product terms to keep the longest path short. Also consider physical wiring and verification: gate-level implementations are easy to simulate but can grow messy for large ISAs. A testing strategy is to exercise each opcode and verify every control output against the truth table. Remember that gate count and gate depth influence both silicon area and the critical path delay; balancing them is a practical part of good implementation. Finally, ensure you include inverters where the equations require negated signals.

keyIdea.title: AND-OR implementation
keyIdea.text: Direct gate wiring follows sums-of-products logic; manage OR fan-in and gate depth to control delay.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › AND-OR Logic
Wiring sums of products
Product terms from decoded signals feed OR gates to produce control outputs.
Practical notes
  • Limit OR gate fan-in by factoring expressions into smaller OR trees.
  • Use inverters where the logic needs negated inputs.
  • Test by comparing outputs for every opcode against the truth table.
Concrete gate example
// Example wiring for RegWrite
// Decoder asserts ADD and LW
RegWrite = OR(ADD, LW)   // two-input OR gate

// ALUSrc = OR(LW, SW)
ALUSrc = OR(LW, SW)
Pro tip
Factor expressions shared across outputs to reduce redundant product terms and lower gate count.

screens.title: Programmable Logic Array (PLA)
screens.narratorSegment: A Programmable Logic Array organizes control logic into two planes: an AND plane that produces product terms and an OR plane that sums selected product terms into outputs. Conceptually, the AND plane lays out horizontal product-term lines composed of decoded signals and possibly state bits. The OR plane has vertical output lines representing control signals; programmable crosspoints connect selected product terms to each output. This regular grid makes PLAs compact and easy to synthesize for control logic because you program product terms once and reuse them across outputs. For a RISC control unit with a small number of instruction types, a PLA is attractive: it reduces wiring complexity compared to a sprawling set of discrete AND and OR gates and simplifies verification. However, PLAs may consume more power for sparse logic and require programming infrastructure during design. Practically, implement a PLA by listing product terms from your truth table and constructing a connection matrix that maps terms to control outputs. The PLA's regular layout also makes it straightforward to estimate the critical path: AND plane delay plus OR plane delay plus any inverter delays.

keyIdea.title: PLA structure
keyIdea.text: A PLA implements sums of products with a programmable AND plane and OR plane, offering a compact, regular implementation for control logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Programmable Logic Array
PLA: AND plane + OR plane
Program product terms in the AND plane and map them to outputs in the OR plane using crosspoints.
Design steps
  1. List all product terms required by the truth table.
  2. Program the AND plane to produce those terms.
  3. Connect product terms to control outputs via the OR plane crosspoints.
When to pick a PLA
Choose PLA for small, dense control functions where regularity and verification simplicity outweigh slightly higher power or area for sparse logic.
Key Takeaway

A PLA is a structured, programmable realization of sums-of-products ideal for compact control logic in RISC processors.

screens.title: Speed vs Flexibility Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Hardwired control gains speed because outputs are produced by combinational logic with minimal gate depth; control signals become available quickly after the opcode is decoded. This makes hardwired control ideal in RISC designs where the ISA is small and stable. On the other hand, hardwired designs are inflexible: changing or adding instructions requires redesigning the logic or reprogramming the PLA. Microcoded control addresses flexibility by implementing control as a sequence of microinstructions stored in ROM; designers can add complex instruction behavior or variable-length instructions without rewiring combinational logic. A common historical example is that early complex CISC machines used microcode to manage hundreds of instructions and addressing modes. The trade-off is performance: microcoded paths often incur extra cycles. When evaluating a design, ask how often the ISA will change and how critical single-instruction latency is. For many embedded RISC processors, the speed advantage outweighs the cost of reduced flexibility. For general-purpose CISC designs with many legacy instructions, microcode simplifies implementation and evolution despite slower execution paths. Speed vs Flexibility Trade-offs means hardwired control yields low-latency signals and simple verification for stable isas; microcode gives flexibility for complex, evolving instruction sets at the cost of extra cycles.. In practical terms, why hardwired control is fast but less flexible than microcode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison at a glance
Hardwired control
Very low-latency outputs, efficient for stable, small ISAs; harder to extend.
Microcoded control
Flexible and easier to implement complex instructions, but adds microcode cycles and can be slower per instruction.
Design questions
  • How often will the ISA change?

screens.title: Design Exercise: Multi-Cycle Control Signals
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on task extends truth table design to a multi-cycle processor with five instruction types and five stages: IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB. For each instruction and each stage list which control signals must be active. For example, during IF the PC must update and the instruction memory is read; during WB the register file is written for ADD and LW. After listing the stage-specific signals, derive Boolean equations for each control output as a function of the instruction-type signals and a 3-bit state counter representing the current stage. That means product terms will include both instruction signals and state bits: RegWrite = (ADD AND WB) OR (LW AND WB). When synthesizing the logic, factor the state bits where possible to reduce duplication. Finally, compute the propagation delay by counting gate levels along the longest path from opcode bits and state bits through decoder, AND plane, OR plane, and output gates, assuming 1 ns per gate. This exercise teaches how stage information integrates with instruction decoding and why PLAs are convenient for multi-cycle control: product terms naturally combine instruction and state signals in the AND plane.

keyIdea.text: Combine instruction-type decoding with stage bits to create stage-aware control equations and calculate gate-level delay.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Multi-Cycle Activity
Step 1 — Stage mapping
For each instruction, list active signals in IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB. Example: ADD asserts RegWrite only in WB.
Example row
ADD: IF(read instruction), EX(ALU compute), WB(RegWrite). LW: MEM(MemRead), WB(RegWrite with MemtoReg).
Step 2 — Equations with state
Derive expressions that include state bits. Example below.
// WB stage is state == 100 for example
RegWrite = (ADD AND WB) OR (LW AND WB)
ALUSrc   = (LW AND EX) OR (SW AND EX)
Key Takeaway

Include state bits in product terms for stage-accurate control. PLAs map these combinations cleanly into an AND plane.

screens.title: Gate Delay Calculation
screens.narratorSegment: To estimate control unit speed, compute the propagation delay along the longest path from opcode bits to a control signal. For a gate-level AND-OR implementation, the critical path typically includes: opcode bits through the decoder, decoder output through any AND gates producing product terms, through OR gates combining product terms, and finally any output buffering or inversion. If we assume 1 nanosecond per gate, sum the gate levels: a decoder may be two gate levels, the AND plane one gate level, and the OR plane another gate level, giving roughly 4 ns before buffering. For a PLA the typical critical path is AND plane delay plus OR plane delay; depending on physical implementation this might be 2 to 4 gate delays. Remember to include inverters where signals are negated; each inverter adds one gate delay. A common mistake is to forget fan-in effects: gates with many inputs may have longer effective delay. Use factoring to reduce levels, or restructure logic into balanced trees. Estimating delay this way gives you a practical bound on how quickly control signals become valid and helps decide if the control unit will meet your cycle time requirements.

keyIdea.title: Delay estimation
keyIdea.text: Sum gate levels along the longest path; include decoder, AND plane, OR plane and any inverters to approximate propagation delay.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Gate Delay Calculation
Estimate the critical path
Assume 1 ns per gate. Count gate levels from opcode to final control signal.
Worked approximation
Decoder: 2 ns, AND plane: 1 ns, OR plane: 1 ns, buffer/inverter: 1 ns → total ≈ 5 ns for a worst-case signal.
Practical tips
  • Factor expressions to reduce gate count and depth.
  • Balance large ORs into trees to avoid single long-delay gates.
  • Include inverters and buffering when summing delays.
Common mistake
Ignoring gate fan-in or physical implementation details leads to optimistic delay estimates. Always add margin.

screens.title: Why PLA is Good for RISC — Short Answer
screens.narratorSegment: When answering why a PLA is a good implementation choice for a hardwired control unit in a RISC processor, highlight regularity, compactness and verification benefits. A PLA structures sums-of-products into two programmable planes: the AND plane produces product terms that combine decoded instruction and state bits, and the OR plane maps these terms to outputs. For a RISC ISA with a small set of instruction types and predictable control patterns, the PLA's regular array reduces wiring complexity compared with discrete AND/OR networks. PLAs are often faster than a complex microcoded path because they compute outputs in a few gate levels. They simplify verification since you can enumerate product terms and check the connection matrix systematically. The trade-off is power and area for sparse implementations, but control logic tends to be dense enough to make PLAs efficient. When composing your answer, include a concrete example: list product terms for LW and ADD and show how both feed RegWrite via the OR plane. End by contrasting PLA maintainability versus the flexibility of microcode so the grader sees you recognize both sides of the trade-off.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore how a hardwired control unit converts an instruction opcode into the control signals that drive every part of the datapath. You will learn what each common signal does, how to build a truth table that maps instruction types to signals, and how to turn that truth table into Boolean equations implemented with AND, OR and NOT gates. We will also examine the programmable logic array, a compact, regular way to implement many control equations, and contrast the performance and flexibility trade-offs compared with microcoded control. A concrete example will show how ADD, LW, SW and BEQ set RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, ALUSrc, MemtoReg, Branch and ALUOp lines. By the end, you should be able to design a truth table for a small instruction set and select an implementation style — gate logic or PLA — based on speed and ease of change. A common misconception is that faster always means more complex; we will see situations where a small, fixed ISA benefits from very fast hardwired logic, and other cases where microcode is the sensible choice. Think about an instruction your processor uses: what signals must it set? That question guides design.

By the end of this chapter you will design a hardwired control unit and reason about its trade-offs. First, you will learn to create a truth table that maps instruction opcodes to the set of control signals required for execution, which is a concrete skill for translating ISA semantics into hardware. Second, you will derive Boolean equations from that truth table and express each control signal as a logical combination of decoded instruction-type signals; this skill directly supports gate-level implementation. Third, you will implement the control logic in hardware either with AND-OR gate networks or by programming a PLA, gaining practical experience with two common implementation patterns. Fourth, you will analyze speed, flexibility, and complexity trade-offs and decide when hardwired control is appropriate versus when microcode is preferable. Each objective includes a short practice — build a truth table for five instructions, derive equations, implement on a PLA schematic, and estimate propagation delay. These objectives matter because control logic governs instruction latency and hardware verification effort. Ask yourself: which objective will help you most when adding a new instruction to an ISA?

This page lays out the concrete practice you will use to verify your competency. Start by designing a truth table for five instructions — ADD, SUB, LW, SW and BEQ — and list the control signals active in each instruction. Next, derive Boolean equations from that truth table and test them by checking each instruction row. Then implement the same equations two ways: by wiring AND and OR gates, and by programming a small PLA with AND and OR planes. Finally, analyze delays by assuming a 1-nanosecond delay per gate and summing gate levels along the longest control path. These exercises teach you how to translate ISA semantics into hardware, how to choose an implementation style, and how to estimate performance. For assessment, you will explain why a PLA is a good choice for RISC and why early CISC designs used microcode. Practicing these tasks builds both design intuition and practical verification skills. Which exercise will you tackle first — truth tables, equations, PLA wiring, or delay calculation?

The control unit orchestrates every step of instruction execution by producing control signals that open and close datapath elements. Concretely, control signals enable register writes, gate ALU inputs, choose memory access, and select the next program counter. For example, when the LW instruction executes, MemRead and MemtoReg must be active so that data memory is read and the loaded word is written back into the register file. When an ADD instruction runs, RegWrite is enabled but MemRead and MemWrite are disabled; ALUSrc selects register operands and the ALU performs addition. A hardwired control unit implements these mappings using purely combinational logic: the opcode is decoded into instruction-type lines and those lines feed combinational expressions that produce each control signal. A common misconception is that the control unit stores behavior like a program — it doesn't. Hardwired control is not sequential microcode; it computes outputs directly from opcode and, for multi-cycle designs, the current state. Understanding this difference is crucial when you interpret why PLAs or gate networks are used for speed and why microcode is used when instructions are complex. Consider: what signals must your processor assert when it executes a load instruction?

A truth table is the explicit mapping from each instruction type to the control signals that must be asserted. Building this table forces you to think through the datapath actions for each instruction. For example, using a small instruction set we list rows for ADD, LW, SW and BEQ and mark whether RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, ALUSrc, MemtoReg and Branch are active. This table also includes ALUOp bits that the ALU control uses to select operations. As you construct the table, check the semantics: loads require a memory read and a register write, stores require a memory write and no register write, arithmetic instructions write registers but do not touch memory, and branches assert Branch but not RegWrite. A frequent error is leaving don't-care values undefined; mark them as X only when the datapath truly ignores the signal. Use the truth table to verify your intuition before deriving equations. Below is a compact, code-style representation of the truth table and the standard row-to-equation correspondence you will use when synthesizing logic. Truth Table: Mapping Instructions to Signals means the truth table is the authoritative mapping of instruction types to control outputs and is the source for boolean equations.. In practical terms, build the table that is the foundation of control logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Once the truth table is complete, derive Boolean equations that express each control signal as a logical sum of product terms corresponding to instruction-type signals. The standard process: first decode the opcode into named signals such as ADD, LW, SW, BEQ. Then, for each control output, list the rows where the output is asserted and create product terms that correspond to those instruction signals. For example, RegWrite is asserted for ADD and LW, so RegWrite = ADD OR LW. ALUSrc is asserted for LW and SW, so ALUSrc = LW OR SW. MemtoReg = LW. Branch = BEQ. For ALUOp you can use bit-level outputs: ALUOp1 = ADD; ALUOp0 = BEQ. Implementing these equations directly with AND and OR gates is straightforward: the decoder provides the instruction signals and the OR plane sums them. A common pitfall is failing to factor common terms when scaling to many instructions — factoring reduces gate count and improves delay. Below is a small set of equations you will implement, and then we will show how a PLA realizes the same sums of products in a structured array.

A decoder translates opcode bit patterns into distinct instruction-type signals such as ADD, LW, SW and BEQ. These decoded lines become the simplest inputs to the control equations. The decoder may be a small combinational block that compares opcode bits and asserts exactly one instruction line for fixed-length opcodes. Using decoded signals simplifies the control equations by removing opcode bit-level conditions from every expression. For example, instead of writing RegWrite = (opcode == binary for ADD) OR (opcode == binary for LW) you implement a decoder that outputs ADD or LW and then RegWrite = ADD OR LW. This separation also helps verification: you can test the decoder independently and then verify that the OR/AND network uses those signals correctly. In multi-cycle designs the decoder outputs are often ANDed with the state bits from the finite state machine so that control signals are asserted only in the correct pipeline stage. A common error is to forget to mask decoded signals by state when control is stage-dependent — this leads to transient or persistent wrong signals. Think through the decoder output for each opcode you expect to support.

Implementing control equations with AND and OR gates is the most direct path from Boolean expressions to hardware. Each product term is an AND of decoded signals (or decoded signals combined with state bits), and OR gates sum the needed product terms for each control output. When you wire the network, consider gate fan-in and gate delays: large multi-input ORs increase propagation delay and may need to be balanced by factoring expressions or using tree structures. For example, RegWrite = ADD OR LW is a simple two-input OR. In contrast, a control signal asserted by many instruction types will produce an OR with many inputs; factor or group product terms to keep the longest path short. Also consider physical wiring and verification: gate-level implementations are easy to simulate but can grow messy for large ISAs. A testing strategy is to exercise each opcode and verify every control output against the truth table. Remember that gate count and gate depth influence both silicon area and the critical path delay; balancing them is a practical part of good implementation. Finally, ensure you include inverters where the equations require negated signals.

A Programmable Logic Array organizes control logic into two planes: an AND plane that produces product terms and an OR plane that sums selected product terms into outputs. Conceptually, the AND plane lays out horizontal product-term lines composed of decoded signals and possibly state bits. The OR plane has vertical output lines representing control signals; programmable crosspoints connect selected product terms to each output. This regular grid makes PLAs compact and easy to synthesize for control logic because you program product terms once and reuse them across outputs. For a RISC control unit with a small number of instruction types, a PLA is attractive: it reduces wiring complexity compared to a sprawling set of discrete AND and OR gates and simplifies verification. However, PLAs may consume more power for sparse logic and require programming infrastructure during design. Practically, implement a PLA by listing product terms from your truth table and constructing a connection matrix that maps terms to control outputs. The PLA's regular layout also makes it straightforward to estimate the critical path: AND plane delay plus OR plane delay plus any inverter delays.

Hardwired control gains speed because outputs are produced by combinational logic with minimal gate depth; control signals become available quickly after the opcode is decoded. This makes hardwired control ideal in RISC designs where the ISA is small and stable. On the other hand, hardwired designs are inflexible: changing or adding instructions requires redesigning the logic or reprogramming the PLA. Microcoded control addresses flexibility by implementing control as a sequence of microinstructions stored in ROM; designers can add complex instruction behavior or variable-length instructions without rewiring combinational logic. A common historical example is that early complex CISC machines used microcode to manage hundreds of instructions and addressing modes. The trade-off is performance: microcoded paths often incur extra cycles. When evaluating a design, ask how often the ISA will change and how critical single-instruction latency is. For many embedded RISC processors, the speed advantage outweighs the cost of reduced flexibility. For general-purpose CISC designs with many legacy instructions, microcode simplifies implementation and evolution despite slower execution paths.
